extracted.intended_audience: proof theorists, logicians, philosophers of mathematics, and mathematicians interested in measures of proof complexity
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and critiquing graph-theoretic measures of proof complexity (notably genus on logical flow graphs and derivation graphs), their relation to discovermental vs verificational complexity, and consequences for purity (cut-free) vs impurity (with cuts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical flow graphs track single-formula movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical flow graphs are designed to track the movement of a single formula through a proof and therefore ignore the structure introduced by logical connectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because they only track atomic formulas (or movement of a single formula), logical flow graphs forget logical inference rules and so "do not capture the global structure of proofs" satisfactorily. Consequently, genus measured on logical flow graphs may miss structural complexity arising from how premises are combined by connectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation graphs capture assumption-discharge relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivation (Statman) graphs represent proofs so as to account for the relationships between any two parts of the proof, including the association between an assumption and the inference that discharges it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By adding assumption-to-discharge edges, derivation graphs aim to represent 'all structural relations between formulas in the proof.' This makes the genus of derivation graphs sensitive to logical rules and to the tree structure of the proof in ways logical flow graphs are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus as a measure of global structural complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Genus of a proof graph is taken to measure the global structural complexity of the associated proof; higher genus indicates a more tightly interwoven inferential network.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statman and Carbone argue that high genus corresponds to many highly interconnected ideas which are harder for a prover/reader to keep track of. Thus genus should reflect difficulty in assembling and surveying the inferential network, not merely size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural rules and structural-like features must be represented
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that parallel structural rules (e.g., contraction, weakening, context-sharing in rules) contribute to genus and so a complexity measure should account for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in systems without explicit structural rules (e.g., some natural deduction presentations), structural effects are present (hidden in inference rules) and affect genus; a measure that ignores these will miss important sources of structural complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical rules (connectives) should affect complexity measure
rubrics_metrics.description: A good measure should be sensitive to the structural effects of logical connectives because their introduction/elimination changes connectivity in the proof graph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carbone's critique is that logical flow graphs ignore structure introduced by logical connectives; derivation graphs do include these effects and hence produce genus changes when formulas are introduced and eliminated, increasing connectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof length measures verificational, not discovermental, complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Length of proof (number of inferences/symbols) is a measure of how hard it is to verify a proof, not necessarily how hard it is to discover a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While cut-free proofs may be longer (verificationally harder), this does not straightforwardly imply they are harder to discover; different measures are needed for discovermental complexity (e.g., genus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity (cut-free) vs impurity (with cuts) must be compared per proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge whether pure or impure proofs are simpler, comparisons should be made between pure and impure proofs of the same proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Global existence results (e.g., 'for every genus n there is a cut-free proof of genus n') do not answer whether, for a given theorem φ, cut-free proofs of φ are systematically more complex than proofs with cut of φ. Good evidence requires proposition-specific comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for lemmas and discharged assumptions in genus calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that use lemmas (proved separately and reused) versus proofs that discharge assumptions affect genus differently: lemmas can increase the upper bound on genus more than discharged assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes upper bounds: replacing assumptions by proofs (lemmas) can raise genus by up to sum m_i g_i, whereas discharging assumptions raises it by at most sum m_i. Thus any complexity measure should track whether resources are packaged as lemmas/cuts or discharged assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine genus with tree-based measures where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Because genus ignores some aspects of the proof tree (size features like number of branches, height, width), a composite measure (genus plus tree measures) may better reflect complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors suggest adding a measure on trees (e.g., number of branches, height, width) to genus so that size-based contributors to complexity are also represented, accommodating those who think size is a necessary contributor to complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying solely on formal symbol-counts for epistemic value
rubrics_metrics.description: The perspicuity and naturality of notions in a proof matter epistemically; pure symbol-count or uninterpreted derivation length is unlikely to provide useful insight alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Avigad and others: formalisations can make ordinary proofs much longer depending on representation choices, so evaluations of proof complexity should attend to conceptual perspicuity, not just raw length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to informal proof outlines and higher-level structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Complexity measures should be applicable not only to fully formal derivations but also to proof-outlines and high-level logical structure as present in mathematical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof-outlines (flow charts, outlines signaling induction or case splits) have logical structure that can be analyzed; measures that can be applied to these outlines are more relevant to actual mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about generalizing existence results to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence-theorems about graphs of arbitrary genus within one class of proofs do not necessarily imply practical patterns of simplicity across pure and impure proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper warns that Carbone's Theorem 3 (there exists for any genus n a cut-free proof of genus n) should not be taken as evidence that impure proofs are generally simpler. One must check whether similar embeddings exist for proofs with cut and make proposition-specific analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize role of propositional/formal methods in contemporary mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures developed for propositional logic and formal derivations can be epistemically relevant because propositional encodings have been crucial in substantial contemporary results (e.g., SAT-solver solution of the Boolean Pythagorean Triples problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This suggests complexity metrics on propositional/formal representations can bear on real mathematical practice; thus defensibility of formal measures requires demonstrating applicability to nontrivial mathematical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-composition and nonessential rule features should be treated carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Some rules (e.g., function composition) can introduce high-degree nodes and affect genus, but they may be eliminable or simulable by other LK rules and so are not essential to a complexity measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes function composition can be removed by constructions and contraction; therefore complexity measures should distinguish between essential structural features and conveniences that can be eliminated without changing core complexity.
